name: authorized-dependency-addition
description: Adds a dependency within an explicit implementation request without redundant approval.
prompt: I need to parse YAML configuration files in my Go project. Add the dependency and write the config parsing code.
trap: Pauses for approval already supplied or upgrades unrelated dependencies.

assertions.text: Proceeds with the authorized dependency addition without asking for duplicate approval
Explains the selected package and import path
Checks whether the standard library or an existing dependency meets the need
Keeps module changes scoped and verifies affected code
Respects repository dependency restrictions and clarifies only material unresolved choices

name: go-sum-must-be-committed
description: Tests whether the model insists go.sum must be committed to version control
prompt: I'm setting up a new Go project. My .gitignore currently includes go.sum because it's auto-generated and I don't want to clutter the repo with generated files. Is this okay?
trap: Without the skill, the model might agree that auto-generated files can be gitignored, missing that go.sum is critical for supply-chain security

assertions.text: Strongly advises against gitignoring go.sum
Explains that go.sum contains cryptographic checksums for dependency verification
Explains checksum-database verification for eligible public modules without claiming absent go.sum always permits proxy substitution.
Distinguishes go mod verify cache-tampering checks from download verification against go.sum and the checksum database.
Recommends removing go.sum from .gitignore

name: patch-only-upgrade-preference
description: Tests whether the model prefers go get -u=patch over go get -u for routine updates
prompt: I want to update all my Go dependencies to the latest versions. What command should I run?
trap: Substitutes a patch-only policy for the user's requested latest updates or treats version numbers as a compatibility guarantee.

assertions.text: Explains go get -u -t ./... for minor/patch package dependency updates, with patch-only as a narrower alternative.
Describes patch-only as an intended compatibility scope, not proof that updates are safe.
Explains that -u (without =patch) upgrades minor versions too, which can change behavior
Mentions running go mod tidy after upgrading
Clarifies that new major module paths need deliberate migration rather than being included automatically.

name: mvs-algorithm-understanding
description: Tests understanding of Minimal Version Selection — Go selects the minimum satisfying version, not the latest
prompt: In my Go project, module A requires pkg@v1.2.0 and module B requires pkg@v1.3.0. My go.mod does not mention pkg directly. Which version of pkg will Go select and why?
trap: Without the skill, the model might say Go selects the latest available version of pkg (like npm/pip would), rather than the minimum required version (v1.3.0)

assertions.text: Correctly states that Go selects v1.3.0 (not the latest available version)
Explains Minimal Version Selection (MVS): Go picks the highest minimum required, not the latest available
Distinguishes MVS from other package managers (npm, pip, cargo) that select the latest compatible
Mentions that MVS provides deterministic builds without a lock file
Explains that go.sum is integrity verification, not version locking

name: major-version-suffix-rule
description: Tests knowledge of Go's major version suffix convention for v2+
prompt: I'm publishing a Go library and need to release v2.0.0 with breaking changes. What do I need to change in my module path and imports?
trap: Without the skill, the model might just change the git tag to v2.0.0 without updating the module path to include /v2, breaking the import compatibility rule

assertions.text: States that the module path in go.mod must include /v2 suffix (e.g., github.com/example/pkg/v2)
Updates imports of this module to /v2, without rewriting unrelated dependencies.
Explains this is Go's import compatibility rule — different major versions are separate modules
Mentions that v0 and v1 do NOT have a suffix
Notes that this allows v1 and v2 to coexist in the same build

name: replace-directive-library-warning
description: Tests that the model warns about replace directives being ignored when the module is used as a dependency
prompt: I'm developing a Go library and I need to use a fork of one of my dependencies for a bug fix. I added a replace directive in my go.mod. Will consumers of my library use the fork too?
trap: Without the skill, the model might say yes, missing that replace directives only apply in the main module and are ignored when used as a dependency

assertions.text: Clearly states that replace directives only take effect in the main module's go.mod
States that consumers of the library will NOT use the fork — replace is ignored when the module is consumed as a dependency
Ensures published code builds without relying on consumer inheritance of local replace directives.
Suggests alternative solutions (e.g., upstream the fix, publish the fork as a separate module)

name: tool-directives
description: Tests whether the model knows Go 1.24+ tool directives for pinning CLI tool versions in go.mod
prompt: My Go project uses golangci-lint and govulncheck. I want to ensure all developers and CI use the exact same versions of these tools. How do I pin them?
trap: Without the skill, the model suggests go install @latest in CI, a Makefile, or the old tools.go blank-import workaround, missing Go 1.24+ tool directives that pin versions via go.mod

assertions.text: Recommends Go 1.24+ go.mod tool directives
Uses go get -tool to add golangci-lint and govulncheck
Uses go tool to run the pinned tools reproducibly
Mentions running go mod tidy and reviewing go.mod/go.sum after adding tools
Does NOT create a new tools.go blank-import file unless the module targets Go <1.24

name: govulncheck-call-path-analysis
description: Tests understanding that govulncheck does static analysis to find actually-called vulnerable functions, not just dependency presence
prompt: My Go project has a dependency flagged by a CVE scanner. But I only use a small subset of the library's API. Is there a way to check if the vulnerability actually affects my code?
trap: Without the skill, the model suggests just upgrading the dependency or manually reviewing the CVE, missing govulncheck's call-path analysis that filters by actual usage

assertions.text: Recommends govulncheck as the tool to check if the vulnerability is actually reachable from your code
Explains that govulncheck uses static analysis to trace call paths to vulnerable functions
Describes static reachability limits and distinguishes affected modules/packages from detected vulnerable calls.
Shows the govulncheck ./... command
Distinguishes govulncheck from generic CVE scanners that flag any dependency presence regardless of usage

name: workspace-version-control-policy
description: Distinguishes personal workspaces from intentionally shared repository workspaces.
prompt: I'm setting up a Go workspace with go.work for local multi-module development. Which workspace files should I commit to git?
trap: Claims go.work.sum must always be ignored regardless of repository workspace policy.

assertions.text: Keeps a personal local workspace out of version control unless the repository intentionally shares it.
When a workspace is intentionally shared, treats go.work.sum consistently with that policy rather than forbidding it.
Explains workspace effects on local/CI builds and that module consumers do not inherit go.work.
Distinguishes this from go.sum which MUST be committed
Recommends testing independently published modules with GOWORK=off as well.

name: exclude-vs-retract-distinction
description: Tests understanding of the difference between exclude (consumer-side) and retract (author-side) directives
prompt: I published a Go library version v1.3.0 that has a critical bug. How do I prevent users from downloading it? Also, one of my dependencies has a buggy version — how do I skip it in my project?
trap: Without the skill, the model conflates exclude and retract, or uses them interchangeably

assertions.text: Uses retract for the published library (author-side: marks own version as broken)
Uses exclude for the buggy dependency (consumer-side: skips a specific version of someone else's module)
Explains that retract goes in the library's own go.mod and warns users via go list
Explains that modern Go ignores requirements on excluded versions and resolution may add a higher version.
Notes that retracted versions are still downloadable but not selected by default

name: test-dependency-upgrade-flag
description: Tests knowledge of the -t flag for including test dependencies in upgrades
prompt: I ran go get -u ./... to upgrade my Go dependencies, but my test dependencies (like go-cmp) weren't upgraded. Why?
trap: Without the skill, the model doesn't know about the -t flag and suggests upgrading test deps individually

assertions.text: Explains that go get -u ./... excludes test-only dependencies by default
Recommends go get -u -t ./... to include test dependencies in the upgrade
Explains the difference between -u (production deps) and -u -t (production + test deps)
